reasoning_traces.think:
The transition from group-based to single-league formats introduces a fundamental shift in how match outcomes influence prize allocation. In the group stage, teams are confined to isolated subgraphs where prize eligibility is determined locally. This creates a natural boundary for competitiveness—matches within a group are only competitive if they affect the top-two finishers. In contrast, the single league format allows for global interdependencies, where even late-stage matches may carry implications for qualification. Using integer programming, the authors model the prize security threshold for each team, identifying when a match outcome no longer affects final standings. Monte Carlo simulations then estimate the frequency of such non-competitive matches under both formats. The derived kernel of competitiveness hinges on the conditional independence of prize outcomes from match results, which is violated when teams are mathematically eliminated or when collusion is possible. This leads to a dualistic view: while the new format increases overall competitive matches, it also raises the risk of collusion due to fewer constraints on match dynamics.
